item.title: Situational Awareness: Reading the Room Before You Read the Contract
item.dc:creator: Ryan Berner
item.description: Why noticing the small, early signals in a showing or negotiation — before they ever show up in writing — is a skill worth bringing to your Flathead Valley home sale.
item.content:encoded:
Situational Awareness: Reading the Room Before You Read the Contract

Here's a question worth sitting with before your next showing or negotiation: by the time a problem shows up in an email or a contract addendum, how long had it actually been building?

Almost always, longer than anyone wanted to admit.

The habit of noticing before it's obvious

In a higher-stakes line of work, you learn to clock small deviations from baseline before they become anything worth reporting — a changed routine, a longer pause than usual, someone standing slightly off from where they normally would. None of it is dramatic in the moment. Most of it is forgettable. But the pattern underneath it tells you something is shifting before anyone says so out loud.

Real estate runs on the same signal, just lower stakes and friendlier terrain. A buyer who lingers an extra two minutes in the primary bedroom isn't nothing. A seller who answers a question about the roof a half-second too fast, or too carefully, isn't nothing either. Neither is the inspector who goes quiet near the crawlspace access instead of narrating like they did everywhere else. None of these are facts you can put in a report. All of them are worth paying attention to.

Why this matters more than people think

Most negotiations don't fall apart over the big, obvious issue — the one everyone saw coming and priced in from day one. They fall apart over the thing nobody named early enough: a buyer who went quiet on a showing and nobody asked why, a seller who kept deflecting a specific question until it finally surfaced as a surprise during inspection, an agent on the other side whose tone shifted two emails before their client actually said they were walking.

By the time any of that lands in writing, it's already a problem to manage instead of a conversation to have. The gap between noticing and reacting is where deals either stay healthy or start quietly eroding.

What this actually looks like in a transaction

This isn't about reading minds, and it isn't about being suspicious of everyone in the room. It's about treating a showing, a counteroffer, or a walkthrough as more than a checklist to get through. A few concrete habits:

In a showing: Watch where people slow down versus where they move through on autopilot. The room they circle back to twice is telling you something about priorities nobody stated out loud — useful information when it comes time to write or respond to an offer.

In negotiation: Notice when a response takes longer than the question warranted, or arrives faster than it should have. Both are data. Neither means panic — it means ask one more question before you answer theirs.

In inspection and disclosure: Pay attention to what someone volunteers without being asked versus what only comes out when pressed. A seller who brings up the well pump issue before the inspector finds it is a different risk profile than one who waits to see if it gets flagged.

In communication cadence: A buyer or seller who normally replies within hours and suddenly takes two days isn't automatically a lost deal — but it's a cue to check in directly instead of assuming silence means disinterest or, worse, assuming it means nothing at all.

None of this replaces the paperwork, the inspection report, or the numbers. It's what happens in the space before those things, where most of the actual leverage and actual risk quietly live.

The part people get backwards

The instinct for a lot of buyers and sellers is to wait for something to become official before reacting to it — to treat a hunch as not worth mentioning until there's a document to point to. That's backwards. The document is the end of the story, not the beginning of it. By the time an issue is in writing, the only options left are damage control. Caught two weeks earlier, in a conversation instead of a contract clause, it's just a Tuesday.

This is also why a transaction benefits from having someone in it whose job is specifically to be paying attention the whole way through — not reactively, after a text message lands with bad news, but continuously, from the first showing to the final walkthrough. That's not a special talent. It's a trained habit, and it transfers cleanly from rooms with a lot more on the line than a Flathead Valley listing.

A question worth sitting with

Think back to the last negotiation, personal or professional, that went sideways. Was there a moment — a pause, a change in tone, a question that got answered a little too smoothly — that you noticed at the time and set aside, only to watch it turn into the actual issue two weeks later? Most people can name the moment once they look for it. The goal isn't hindsight. It's catching that moment while there's still time to do something useful with it.

If you're heading into a sale or a purchase in Kalispell or Whitefish and want someone paying attention to more than just the numbers on the page, that's exactly the conversation worth having early.

item.title: When the Appraisal Comes in Low: A Flathead Seller's Real Options
item.dc:creator: Ryan Berner
item.description: Your buyer's appraisal came in under contract price. Here's what actually happens next for a Kalispell or Whitefish seller, and the four real paths forward.
item.content:encoded:
When the Appraisal Comes in Low: A Flathead Seller's Real Options

You've got a signed contract. The buyer is financing, the inspection went fine, and then the lender's appraisal comes back under your agreed price. Before you assume the deal is dead or that you have to eat the difference, here's what's actually happening and what you can do about it.

Why this happens more often in a market like ours

An appraisal isn't an opinion of what a buyer is willing to pay — it's a lender's check that the collateral supports the loan, built off recent closed comparable sales. In a Flathead market where days on market have stretched out and price cuts have become more common on listings that sat too long, the comps an appraiser pulls can lag behind what an eager buyer just agreed to pay, especially on a property with real character: lake frontage, acreage, a custom build, or anything else that doesn't have a clean twin that closed in the last six months. The gap isn't usually a sign you overpriced the home. It's often a sign the appraisal process is backward-looking in a market that's still finding its footing.

What the contract actually says happens next

Montana purchase contracts typically include a financing contingency, and inside that, an appraisal condition that gives the buyer an out if the home doesn't appraise at or above the contract price. That contingency protects the buyer, not you — which is exactly why sellers who don't read it closely get caught off guard. It does not automatically cancel the deal, and it does not automatically mean you have to lower your price. It means the buyer now has a decision to make, and so do you.

Your four real options

Challenge the appraisal. This is the first move, and it's underused. Your agent can submit a reconsideration of value with better comps — recent closings the appraiser missed, pending sales that support the number, or documentation on upgrades and unique features that a drive-by comparison undervalues. This works more often than sellers expect, particularly on properties with acreage, outbuildings, or finishes that are hard to quantify from the street.

Split the difference. If the gap is modest, meeting the buyer partway on price is often the fastest path to closing without either side feeling like they lost. This is a negotiation, not a concession — know your number before you're in the conversation, not during it.

Ask the buyer to bring the difference in cash. Some buyers can and will cover the gap between the appraised value and the contract price out of pocket to keep the deal and the lower rate they locked. It's a reasonable ask, especially if the buyer has shown strong motivation throughout the transaction. It's not guaranteed, but it costs you nothing to put on the table.

Let the contingency do its job. If the numbers genuinely don't work for either side, the appraisal contingency allows the buyer to walk and get their earnest money back. That's a real outcome, and sometimes the right one — but it's worth knowing it's the last option, not the first, before anyone defaults to it.

What a seller should not do

Don't treat a low appraisal as proof your asking price was wrong and reflexively drop it to match. An appraisal is one data point from one appraiser working off one set of comps on one day. It is not the market's final word, and plenty of homes that appraised low on a first pass have closed at or near the original contract price once the value got challenged or the buyer found a way to bridge the gap. Don't skip reading your own contract's appraisal language either — knowing your exact rights and deadlines before the number comes in gives you room to respond instead of react.

The move that actually protects you

Have this conversation with your agent before you're under contract, not after an appraisal surprises you. Know going in what comps support your price, what your walk-away number is if a buyer asks you to come down, and whether the buyer's lender has any flexibility built in. A seller who's thought through the appraisal scenario in advance negotiates from a position of clarity. A seller who's hearing about it for the first time from a panicked phone call is negotiating from behind.

A question worth sitting with

If your home went under contract today, do you know which comps your agent would use to challenge a low number — or would you be starting from zero the moment the appraisal landed? That's a five-minute conversation now that can save you a very stressful week later.

item.title: Kila and the West Valley: The Quiet Corner Most Newcomers Never Look At
item.dc:creator: Ryan Berner
item.description: A look at the Kila/West Valley corridor west of Kalispell — acreage, drive times, schools, and river access most newcomers overlook.
item.content:encoded:
Kila and the West Valley: The Quiet Corner Most Newcomers Never Look At

If you ask someone moving to the Flathead Valley where they're looking, you'll hear the same two or three names almost every time: Whitefish, Bigfork, maybe Lakeside if they want the lake. Ask about Kila and the West Valley corridor, and you'll usually get a pause — "where's that?" — followed by a quick dismiss once they realize it isn't on the water or walking distance to a ski hill.

That's exactly why it's worth a second look.

Where it actually is

Kila sits along US Highway 2 West, roughly a fifteen- to twenty-minute drive from downtown Kalispell, in the broad agricultural and timber country that spreads out toward Marion and the Thompson Falls corridor. The West Valley area — the unincorporated stretch of county between Kalispell's city limits and Kila proper — is close enough to town to make a grocery run or a kid's practice a non-event, but far enough out that the lot sizes, the road noise, and the number of visible neighbors all change.

If you're picturing something remote, recalibrate. This isn't backcountry. It's a working rural corridor with pavement, a post office, a community park, and a steady trickle of daily commuter traffic heading into Kalispell each morning — it just doesn't get talked about the way the postcard towns do.

What the land actually offers

The defining feature of Kila and the West Valley isn't a single landmark — it's spacing. Lot sizes here commonly run from one or two acres up into the twenties and beyond, a different conversation entirely from a quarter-acre in-town lot or a tightly platted subdivision near Whitefish. That space translates into a few concrete things a buyer can actually use: room for outbuildings, horses or livestock where zoning and covenants allow, a real buffer between your porch light and your neighbor's, and night skies that don't wash out the way they do closer to the highway corridor.

The corridor also sits close to the Stillwater and Thompson River drainages, which matters if fishing access, hunting proximity, or simply having public land and river bottom within a short drive is part of why you're looking in the Flathead at all. You don't have to live on the water to benefit from being near it — a twenty-minute drive to a put-in is a different lifestyle than a ninety-minute one.

The commute math people get wrong

The most common mistake newcomers make is assuming "farther from Kalispell" scales linearly with "farther from everything." It doesn't, because the West Valley sits on a direct highway corridor rather than down a winding secondary road. A property near Kila can put you into downtown Kalispell in roughly the same drive time as some in-town-adjacent neighborhoods that feel closer on a map but sit behind slower surface streets and school-zone traffic. Compare that honestly against Bigfork or Whitefish commute times during summer tourist season, when Highway 93 and 35 both slow to a crawl, and the math shifts further in Kila's favor for anyone whose daily life actually centers on Kalispell — work, schools, the hospital, the airport.

Schools and daily logistics

The West Valley area is served by its own elementary school district, with families typically transitioning to Kalispell's secondary schools from there — worth confirming directly with the district for any specific address, since boundary lines don't always follow what a map suggests. For day-to-day logistics, you're close enough to Kalispell for groceries, healthcare, and Glacier Park International Airport to stay convenient, while still getting the acreage-and-quiet trade-off that draws people out of town in the first place.

Who this fits, by what the property offers

This isn't the corridor for someone whose priority is walking to a coffee shop or a lake dock out the back door — that's a legitimate set of priorities, and Whitefish or Bigfork likely serves them better. Kila and the West Valley fit a different set of priorities: more land for the money, a shorter commute than the acreage would suggest, proximity to river and public-land access, and a quieter daily baseline without giving up a reasonable drive to town. If those are the things on your list, it's worth putting this corridor on your tour — not as a fallback after Whitefish gets too expensive, but as a legitimate first choice.

A question worth sitting with

If you're weighing acreage against commute time, or wondering whether "closer to Kalispell" and "more space" are actually mutually exclusive in this market, that's exactly the kind of question worth walking through before you start touring — not after you've fallen for a property that doesn't fit the rest of your life.

item.title: How Long Montana Probate Actually Takes Before a House Can List
item.dc:creator: Ryan Berner
item.description: Why a home can't list the week after a death, and the realistic probate timeline Flathead Valley families should expect before a listing agreement is enforceable.
item.content:encoded:
How Long Montana Probate Actually Takes Before a House Can List

If someone just passed away and you're already being asked when the house will "go on the market," here's the question worth sitting with first: who actually has the legal authority to sign the listing agreement right now? For most families, the honest answer is nobody — not yet.

That catches people off guard. The assumption is usually that a home can list within a week or two of a funeral, as soon as the family agrees it's time. In practice, Montana probate has to hand someone formal authority to act on the estate's behalf before a listing agreement is worth the paper it's signed on. Here's what that timeline realistically looks like, and what tends to add weeks to it.

Why "right after the funeral" isn't how this works

A house doesn't become sellable the moment someone is gone — it becomes sellable once a personal representative (Montana's term for what some states call an executor or administrator) is formally appointed by the court and holds documented authority over the estate's assets, including the real property. Until that happens, no one can bind the estate to a listing agreement, a purchase and sale contract, or a closing. That's true even when every heir agrees on the plan and even when the family already has a buyer lined up informally.

This isn't bureaucracy for its own sake. It exists so that whoever signs on the estate's behalf can actually convey clear title — which is what both the buyer's lender and the title company will insist on before closing regardless of how eager everyone is to move.

Informal vs. formal probate — the fork that decides your timeline

Montana offers two main tracks, and which one applies has the biggest effect on how long this takes.

Informal probate is the faster, more common path when there's a valid will (or a clear path under intestacy law), no real dispute among heirs, and nothing unusual about the estate. A district court clerk — not a judge — can appoint the personal representative, often within a few weeks of filing. Once appointed, the PR receives Letters Testamentary (with a will) or Letters of Administration (without one), which is the actual document a listing agreement and a buyer's title company will want to see.

Formal probate gets involved when there's a will contest, uncertainty about who the rightful heirs are, disagreement over who should serve as personal representative, or other complications. This track requires a judge, often a hearing, and routinely adds a month or more before anyone is appointed — sometimes considerably longer if the dispute is contested.

Most straightforward family situations in the Flathead qualify for informal probate. But "most" isn't "all," and it's worth finding that out early rather than assuming.

What "authority to sign" actually looks like on paper

Letters Testamentary or Letters of Administration are what a listing brokerage and, later, a title company will ask to see before treating a sale as real. Until those are issued, a family can still prepare the house, gather documents, get it appraised, or have informal conversations with an agent about pricing and timing — but the listing agreement itself isn't enforceable, and a buyer's lender won't move toward closing on a contract that no one had the authority to sign.

Practically, that means the useful early work — decluttering, minor repairs, pulling together the deed and tax records, deciding on a target price range — doesn't have to wait on the court. The signature does.

The creditor-claim window, and what else adds weeks

Once a personal representative is appointed, Montana law requires a notice-to-creditors period, giving the estate's creditors a window to file claims before certain distributions are considered final. That window runs in parallel with marketing the home, so it rarely blocks a listing outright — but it's one more piece of the overall timeline families don't always know to expect.

Beyond that, a few things reliably add real weeks to a probate sale:

A missing or unclear will forces the informal path toward formal probate, since the court needs to sort out who the proper heirs are before anyone gets appointed. Out-of-state heirs can slow things down when documents require notarized signatures or in-person steps that take longer to coordinate remotely. And disagreement among heirs — even mild, well-intentioned disagreement about price, timing, or whether to sell at all — is probably the single most common delay, because it can push an otherwise informal case toward formal proceedings.

Knowing which of these applies to your situation early is what keeps a family from guessing for weeks before finding out the real timeline.

Where this leaves a family

None of this is a reason to wait to start preparing — it's a reason to find out, early, which track your situation is actually on. An estate attorney confirms the specifics for your probate; this is a starting orientation, not a determination of your case.

So here's the question worth asking before anything else: has a personal representative actually been appointed yet, or is that step still in progress? If you're not sure, that's a completely normal place to be — and a good first conversation to have before you start planning around a listing date.

item.title: New Construction vs. Resale in the Flathead: What the Timeline Actually Looks Like
item.dc:creator: Ryan Berner
item.description: Comparing a new build to a resale home in Kalispell or Whitefish? Here's how the real timelines compare — permitting, builder queues, rate locks, and closing dates.
item.content:encoded:
New Construction vs. Resale in the Flathead: What the Timeline Actually Looks Like

If you're cross-shopping a new-build lot against a resale house in Kalispell or Whitefish, chances are you've already run the price numbers three different ways. Here's the question most buyers don't ask until they're three months in: what does the calendar actually look like on each path?

Price gets compared line by line. Timeline usually doesn't — and timeline is where new construction quietly changes the whole plan, from your rate lock to your lease end date to whether you're moving in before or after the first hard freeze.

The resale timeline, in plain numbers

A resale purchase in this market typically closes in 30 to 45 days from an accepted offer, assuming financing, appraisal, and inspection all move on schedule. That window is fairly predictable because the house already exists — there's no permitting, no framing schedule, no weather delay on a foundation pour. Your lender, title company, and inspector are working against a known structure, not a set of blueprints.

That predictability is the resale trade-off: you know the finish level, the layout, and the move-in date within a few days, almost from the moment your offer is accepted.

What actually stretches a new-build timeline

New construction in Flathead County runs through a few checkpoints that a resale skips entirely, and each one is a place the calendar can slip:

Permitting. Depending on the jurisdiction and whether the lot is inside city limits or in the county, permit review can take anywhere from a few weeks to a couple of months before a builder can break ground. This is almost entirely outside your control and outside the builder's, too — it's queue-dependent on the permitting office.

The builder's queue. Even a builder you trust is working multiple jobs at once. Ask directly where your build sits in that queue and get a realistic start date in writing, not a verbal estimate. "We'll get to it this fall" is not a start date.

Change orders. Every upgrade, every "let's move that outlet," every substituted material because the original is backordered — each one can add both cost and calendar time. A single significant change order can push a close date by weeks, especially if it involves anything structural or requires re-ordering materials.

Weather. Flathead Valley winters are real. A foundation that should have been poured in September but gets pushed to November because of permitting delays is now racing the ground freeze, and that alone can add a season to the build.

Put together, a realistic new-construction timeline in this market often runs six months to well over a year from signed contract to move-in — compared to 30-45 days for a comparable resale. That's not a knock on new construction. It's the honest gap buyers need to plan around.

Where a rate lock fits into this

If you're financing, your rate lock matters more on new construction than most buyers expect. A standard lock might run 30 to 60 days — nowhere close to covering a build that could take six months or longer. Builders often work with a lender who offers an extended or "lock-and-shop" product designed for construction timelines, but that's a conversation to have before you sign a builder contract, not after your original lock has already expired and you're staring at a higher rate.

Ask your lender directly: "What happens to my rate if this build runs past my lock window?" Get the answer in writing before you commit.

HOA and covenant review — new developments vs. established neighborhoods

New developments often come with a fresh HOA, and "fresh" means the covenants, fees, and enforcement track record don't have years of history to review yet. Compare that to an established Kalispell or Whitefish neighborhood, where you can actually see how an HOA has behaved — its fee history, its reserve fund, how it's handled maintenance or disputes. On a new development, you're reviewing what's written on paper with less real-world track record to check it against. Read the covenants closely, and ask what's actually funded in the reserve account versus what's projected.

So which one is right for you?

This isn't a case against new construction — plenty of buyers have very good reasons to want it: nothing to renovate, current building codes, a floor plan built around exactly how they live. The point is picking with your eyes open on time, not just price.

If you need to be in a home by a specific date — a lease ending, a school year starting, a job relocation — that alone might settle the question. If your timeline has real flexibility and you want a home built exactly to your spec, new construction might be worth the wait.

Where are you actually flexible on your move-in date, and where are you not? That question usually clarifies the decision faster than another round of price comparisons.

item.title: Why Divorcing Couples Should Use One Listing Agent
item.dc:creator: Ryan Berner
item.description: When a marital home goes on the market, each spouse hiring a separate agent feels like protection. In practice it usually costs money and slows the sale. Here's how a single neutral agent actually works.
item.content:encoded:
Why Divorcing Couples Should Use One Listing Agent

Somewhere in the first conversation about selling the house, someone usually asks a version of the same question: should we each bring our own agent to this?

It's a reasonable instinct. If the attorneys are separate, why wouldn't the agents be too?

Here's what I tell people, and why it's not the answer that makes me the most money: for a single marital home going to market, one neutral listing agent almost always serves both spouses better than two competing ones. Not because two agents can't be professional with each other — most can — but because of what the structure itself does to price, speed, and how much of this you have to relive.

Two agents usually means dual agency problems or a diluted commission

There are really only two ways "each spouse has their own agent" plays out on a single listing, and neither is what people picture.

One version: both agents are technically working the same listing, splitting one commission, each reporting back to their own client. That's slower by design — every decision routes through two filters instead of one, and disagreements between the spouses get amplified by disagreements between their agents, who each have an incentive to look like they're advocating hard for their side.

The other version, more common than people expect: one spouse's "own agent" ends up representing the buyer instead, once it's clear there's only one listing to be had. Now you have one agent on the sale and one on the purchase side, which is a normal transaction structure — but it's not the protection either spouse thought they were getting when they made the call.

Neither version changes the sale price. The house is worth what it's worth. What changes is how much friction, delay, and duplicated explanation gets built into getting there.

What a neutral agent actually does differently

A single agent working directly for both of you isn't a compromise position — it's a specific set of protocols, and I tell both spouses what they are before either signs anything.

Same information, same time, always in writing. Price opinions, showing feedback, offer summaries, inspection findings — one document, sent to both parties and both attorneys at once. No version of the numbers that one spouse sees first.

No side conversations about strategy. Either spouse can call me with a question about the process, and I'll answer it. What I won't do is take a call about how to get a better outcome from the other spouse. That's not neutrality with an asterisk — it's the whole point.

Pricing gets set on the comps, not on who wants what number. In an ordinary sale, a seller can chase a number for emotional reasons and it's their call to make. In a divorce sale, one spouse wanting to list high to "not leave money on the table" and the other wanting to list low to be done with it are both, in effect, asking the agent to take a side. Neither request moves the listing price. The comparable sales do.

One person accountable for the whole file. When something needs a decision — a repair request, a closing date that conflicts with one spouse's move, a buyer asking for a rent-back — there's one person who has the complete picture and gets it in front of both of you at once, instead of two agents each working from half the story.

Where this actually saves money

The commission math is the most direct case for it. Splitting one listing's commission across two agents doesn't cost either spouse a discount — it just means two people are doing the coordination work that one person can do for the same total fee. That's not the strongest reason to do it, but it's a real one, and it's worth saying plainly since it's often the last thing anyone mentions.

The bigger cost is time. A stalled or mismanaged sale carries a mortgage payment, insurance, utilities, and property tax every month it drags — split, disputed, or simply unpaid while everyone waits for someone else to move first. A structure that gets to a clean closing faster is worth more than the commission split either way.

What this doesn't decide

To be clear about the boundary: whether to sell at all, how the proceeds get divided, whether one spouse buys the other out instead — those are questions for your attorneys and, if it comes to it, the court. A neutral agent runs the listing well. A neutral agent doesn't decide what's fair, and I'm not going to pretend otherwise or offer legal or tax guidance I'm not licensed to give. Consult your attorney or CPA on anything touching the divorce settlement itself.

What a neutral agent can do is remove the real estate transaction as one more thing you're litigating through two separate lenses — so the parts that do need your attorneys get your attorneys' full attention, instead of competing with a listing dispute for it.

A question worth asking before you each call an agent

If you pictured the sale finished and the keys handed over, would having gone through two competing agents have made that outcome better, or just made the six months before it harder?

If you're weighing this decision right now, I'm glad to walk you through exactly how a neutral listing works before either of you commits to anything. No pressure, and nothing gets listed because we talked.

item.title: New Listings vs. Pending: The Ratio That Shows Who Has the Leverage
item.dc:creator: Ryan Berner
item.description: Days on market gets all the attention, but the ratio between new listings and pending sales moves first. Here's what it's telling Flathead buyers and sellers right now.
item.content:encoded:
New Listings vs. Pending: The Ratio That Shows Who Has the Leverage

Most people watching the Flathead market check one number: how long is this house going to sit. Days on market is useful, but it's a lagging indicator — it tells you what already happened to a listing, not what's about to happen to the market underneath it.

There's a better number, and almost nobody outside the industry watches it: the ratio between new listings and pending sales. It moves before price does, and before days-on-market does, because it's measuring something more basic — is fresh supply outrunning demand, or is demand eating supply faster than it's arriving.

The Current Numbers

As of today, Flathead County has 95 new listings currently on the market against 368 homes in pending status — under contract, working their way to closing (Redfin county-level data, live as of September 28, 2026).

Run that as a ratio and you get roughly one new listing for every 3.9 homes already locked into a pending contract. Put differently: for every fresh property landing on the market this week, close to four others are already off the table, just waiting to close.

That's a meaningfully lopsided ratio, and it's worth comparing against the backdrop most Flathead readers already know: countywide median days on market sat at 77 in the most recent monthly read, up from 62 a year ago (Movoto Kalispell market data, period through August 2026). Those two facts look like they're pulling in opposite directions — a slower market on one hand, a pending pipeline that dwarfs new supply on the other — and that tension is exactly the point. Days on market measures how long the average listing has been sitting, including the ones that are struggling. The new-listings-to-pending ratio measures the front door and the back door of the market at the same time, right now, and right now the back door — homes going under contract — is moving a lot more inventory than the front door is bringing in.

What a Ratio This Lopsided Actually Telegraphs

When pending sales run this far ahead of new listings, it usually means one of two things is happening, and it pays to know which one you're standing in.

The first possibility: real demand is absorbing inventory faster than sellers are willing to list, which tightens the market for buyers even while headline days-on-market numbers look soft. A buyer waiting on the sidelines for "more to choose from" may be waiting on a shrinking pool, not a growing one — the well-priced, well-prepared listings are getting picked off into pending status well before the average 77-day clock runs out, and what's left sitting on the market disproportionately skews toward the properties that are overpriced or otherwise sticky. If that's the case, the buyers who move now, on the right house, are the ones who benefit. The buyers who wait for the market to "come to them" may find the ratio has already told them the good inventory left first.

The second possibility: a batch of pendings from earlier in the summer is finally working through financing and appraisal and hasn't closed yet, inflating the pending count relative to a genuinely slower new-listing flow this particular week. That's a timing artifact, not a trend — and it's exactly why this is a number to watch over a few weeks, not read off a single Tuesday.

Either way, the ratio is the earliest signal either side gets. Price adjusts last. Days-on-market adjusts second. The new-listings-to-pending ratio is the one that moves first, because it's counting behavior — sellers deciding to list, buyers deciding to commit — instead of counting outcomes.

The Rate Backdrop

None of this happens in a vacuum. Freddie Mac's Primary Mortgage Market Survey put the 30-year fixed rate at 7.03% for the week ending September 24, 2026, up from 6.95% the week before and well above the 6.30% average from the same week a year ago. A rate that's climbed roughly three-quarters of a point year-over-year is part of why sellers are more cautious about listing right now — trading a known rate for an unknown one is a real cost — which helps explain the thin new-listings side of this week's ratio even as pending activity holds up.

What To Do With This This Week

If you're a seller watching your neighbor's listing sit at day 40 or 50 and wondering whether the market has stalled: the ratio says otherwise. Demand hasn't disappeared — it's just being more selective about which listings it's absorbing into pending status, and the ones getting picked are the ones priced and presented correctly the first time.

If you're a buyer waiting for a bigger pool to shop from: this week's numbers suggest the opposite is more likely. The properties disappearing into "pending" are outnumbering the ones showing up "new" by nearly four to one. Waiting for more selection, in this particular ratio environment, may just mean watching the same properties you'd have wanted go under contract without you.

Neither of those is a reason to rush a decision you're not ready to make. It's a reason to know which side of the ratio you're actually standing on before you decide to wait.

Curious what this ratio looks like for your specific price band or neighborhood, rather than the countywide number? That's a five-minute conversation, not a sales pitch.

item.title: Radio Discipline: Why Clients Get a Weekly Update, Not Just the Big News
item.dc:creator: Ryan Berner
item.description: Why every client gets a standing update whether or not there's anything to report — and what that discipline is actually built to prevent.
item.content:encoded:
Radio Discipline: Why Clients Get a Weekly Update, Not Just the Big News

There's a habit that gets trained into you early in high-stakes work, and it has nothing to do with real estate on its face: you report in on schedule, whether or not you have anything to say.

In the kind of work I came from, silence on the radio was never read as good news. It was read as the opposite — as a break in contact, a gap nobody could account for. The whole point of a scheduled check-in wasn't to deliver big news. Most of the time there wasn't any. The point was that the absence of an update, on schedule, is itself information, and it's the kind of information that makes people start assuming the worst. So you report in anyway. "Nothing to report" is a complete sentence, and it's a useful one.

I still run that way. Every client of mine gets a standing weekly update — a real one, not a form email — whether or not there's a showing, an offer, or a document to sign that week. Here's why that's a rule and not a nicety.

What the Three-Week Silence Actually Does

Picture a listing that's been on the market five weeks. Showings were steady the first two, then they slowed, the way they do. Nothing dramatic has happened. Nobody's called with news because there isn't any news — no offer, no feedback worth flagging, no change in strategy.

To the agent, that's an ordinary week. To the seller sitting at home watching the listing count days on Zillow, three weeks without a word from their agent doesn't read as "nothing happening." It reads as "nobody's paying attention to my house anymore." That gap gets filled with a worse story than the truth almost every time — the agent's lost interest, the price is wrong and nobody wants to say it, the market's dead and nobody's telling me. None of that has to be true for the seller to start believing it. The silence does the work on its own.

The same thing happens on the buy side, especially during a financing contingency or an inspection response that's taking longer than expected because the other side is slow, not because anything is wrong. A buyer who hears nothing for two weeks in the middle of that stretch isn't reassured by the quiet. They're bracing for bad news that hasn't arrived yet and might never arrive at all.

The Update That Says Nothing, on Purpose

A weekly check-in that just says "still nothing new, here's what we're watching for next" sounds almost too simple to matter. It matters anyway, for a reason that has nothing to do with the content of the message and everything to do with the fact that it showed up on schedule.

What it actually does: it moves the responsibility for staying informed off the client and onto the process. Nobody has to wonder whether to call and ask "is everything okay?" — because the answer arrives before the question does. It also does something quieter: it establishes, week over week, that if something did go wrong, the client would hear about it the same way, on the same rhythm, without having to chase it down. That's the trust that actually gets tested — not in the easy weeks, but in the one where there's a real problem to report, because by then the client already knows what "Ryan tells me things" looks like in practice.

What This Isn't

It isn't a template email with a mail-merge field for the address. It isn't manufacturing false urgency to look busy, and it isn't padding a report with activity that didn't actually happen — a seller can tell the difference between "here's what actually occurred" and filler, and filler erodes the same trust it's trying to build. The discipline is specifically about showing up on the schedule with the truth, even when the truth is "quiet week, here's what's next," not about generating noise.

It also isn't reserved for the complicated files. Every client gets it — the straightforward resale closing in three weeks and the estate sale working through probate and the divorce sale where both parties are reading the same update on the same day so neither one wonders what the other one was told. The standard doesn't flex based on how easy the file is. That's what makes it a standard instead of a courtesy.

The Actual Point

None of this is about being available around the clock, though the office line is answered that way. It's about a client never having to wonder, mid-week, whether anyone's still working on their behalf. The update on schedule is the answer to that question before it gets asked — which, in the stretches that feel the longest, from a divorce timeline to a slow month on the market, is usually the thing that matters most.

If you're working with someone right now and you can't remember the last time you heard from them without reaching out first, that's worth paying attention to — whether or not there's "big news" to report.

item.title: The First Price Cut: How Long to Wait, and How Much
item.dc:creator: Ryan Berner
item.description: Holding your price and waiting for the market to come to you sounds patient. In today's Flathead market, it usually just means a longer, more expensive path to the same number. Here's how to time and size the first cut instead.
item.content:encoded:
The First Price Cut: How Long to Wait, and How Much

Every seller gets the same advice when a listing goes quiet: give it more time. Don't panic. The right buyer is out there.

That advice isn't wrong, exactly. It's just incomplete, and in the current Kalispell and Whitefish market, incomplete advice gets expensive. The sellers I watch close nearest to their actual number aren't the ones who held their price the longest. They're the ones who moved once, early, and moved enough to matter.

Two Different Questions, One Bad Habit

"Should I cut my price?" isn't really one question. It's two — how long do I wait and how much do I cut — and most sellers answer both of them by feel instead of by evidence. They wait because waiting feels safer than admitting the number might be wrong. Then, when they finally move, they cut just enough to feel like they did something, which is usually the worst amount: too small to reach a new pool of buyers, too public not to signal that the house is struggling.

Treat them as two separate decisions, each with its own answer, and the whole process gets a lot less emotional.

How Long to Wait

The honest answer is shorter than most sellers want to hear, and it's shorter than it was a year ago. Earlier this week I wrote about Kalispell's median days on market stretching to 77, up from 62 a year ago (source: Movoto Kalispell market data, period through August 2026, page updated September 21, 2026). That number isn't just a market snapshot — it's the clock every listing is actually running against now, whether the seller has looked at it or not.

Here's what that means in practice: your first two to three weeks on market are the only period where you're seeing your true audience. Every buyer actively searching your price band and area sees a new listing in that window — saved searches fire, agents preview, the algorithm gives you its best push. That audience doesn't come back a second time with the same energy. If showings are thin and the ones you get don't return for a second look in that window, that's not a sign to wait longer. It's the answer.

Waiting past three weeks with no meaningful activity doesn't buy you more information — it buys you a listing that's aged into "still here" on a buyer's search, competing against houses that are new. At 77 days as the current median, a house that's already sitting at day 30 with no traction isn't halfway through a normal process. It's telling you something the calendar can't fix.

What a Too-Small Cut Actually Signals

This is where sellers lose the most value without realizing it. A five-thousand-dollar trim on a $650,000 listing doesn't reach a single new buyer — most search filters work in round increments, and a cut that doesn't cross one of those thresholds is invisible to anyone who isn't already watching your listing.

But it isn't invisible to the people who are watching. Agents tracking the MLS see a small reduction and read it correctly: a seller testing the water, expecting to cut again. Buyers who've already toured and passed see the same thing and wait, betting there's another cut coming before they need to act. A small first cut doesn't create urgency. It advertises that patience will be rewarded — which means the next offer you get, if one comes at all, tends to come in low, anchored to the number you'll probably drop to next.

The sellers who cut once and move on are the ones who size that first cut to actually change who sees the house, not just to move the number on the listing sheet.

Sizing the Cut Off Comparables, Not a Round Number

The fix isn't cutting bigger for the sake of it — it's cutting off the right information. Pull what's actually closed within roughly a mile in the last 60 to 90 days, not what's currently listed and not what a neighbor claims they were offered in conversation. Closings are evidence. Everything else is a guess dressed up as a data point.

Once you have that number, size your reduction to land your listing in front of a different search bracket entirely — below a round threshold buyers actually filter on, not a few thousand dollars under where you started. A house that moves from $749,000 to $739,000 hasn't changed who sees it. The same house moving to $725,000 has. One clean move that crosses a real line does more than three small ones that never do, and it costs you less in perception each time, because there's only one move to explain instead of a pattern to defend.

The Practical Version

If you're inside your first three weeks, watch traffic and second visits, not the calendar. If you're past that window with thin activity, the question isn't whether to move — it's how far, measured against what's actually closed nearby, not what feels fair. One deliberate cut, sized correctly and made early, beats three apologetic ones every time.

So here's the question worth sitting with if your listing has gone quiet: are you waiting because the data says wait, or because moving the number feels like admitting something you'd rather not?

item.title: Elk Camp and Closing Dates: What Hunting Season Does to a Flathead Calendar
item.dc:creator: Ryan Berner
item.description: Archery season opened September 5 and backcountry rifle districts are already in. Here's what that actually does to inspections, showings, and closing dates across the Flathead Valley right now.
item.content:encoded:
Elk Camp and Closing Dates: What Hunting Season Does to a Flathead Calendar

Archery season opened September 5. A handful of backcountry districts — 150, 280, and 316 — are already into their general rifle season, weeks ahead of the statewide rifle opener on October 24. If you're buying or selling in the Flathead Valley right now, that's not background noise. For a real share of the people on both sides of a transaction, the next several weeks run on a hunting calendar as much as a closing calendar, whether their agent has noticed or not.

I hunt this valley myself, so this isn't a lifestyle piece written from the outside looking in. It's the same discipline I brought to scheduling movements and coordinating with people who weren't always reachable — applied to something lower-stakes, but with the same basic problem: if you build a plan assuming everyone's phone works and everyone's available "whenever," that plan breaks the first time it meets reality.

Where This Shows Up First: Showings

A listing agent who sets a showing window without asking about hunting plans is going to eat a few no-shows this month, and more in October. It's not that buyers and sellers are being difficult — it's that "available anytime" quietly stops being true for a meaningful slice of the valley starting in September and doesn't fully reset until well into November.

The fix is simple and it's the same one I use for anything with a hard deadline: ask early, and ask specifically. Not "are you around this month," but "are there dates you're out of cell range, and dates you know you're back." A seller who tells you October 24–28 is elk camp isn't giving you a scheduling headache — they're giving you the information that keeps a showing from getting booked into a week that was never going to work.

Where It Actually Bites: Inspections and Walkthroughs

Showings are an inconvenience if you get the timing wrong. Inspections and final walkthroughs are different — they sit on a contract with dates attached, and Montana purchase agreements don't pause for opening weekend.

If a buyer or seller is going to be in the backcountry during an inspection contingency window, that needs to be flagged before the offer is written, not discovered three days before the deadline. The same goes for a final walkthrough scheduled against a closing date — if the seller who needs to be present is going to be miles from a cell tower, that's a conversation for the purchase agreement's timeline, not a last-minute scramble with a title company waiting on a signature.

None of this is complicated. It just has to happen on purpose. I build every closing calendar around the assumption that at least one person involved — buyer, seller, sometimes both — has a week where they're genuinely unreachable, and I plan the contingency deadlines and walkthrough dates around that instead of hoping it doesn't come up.

What a Realistic October Looks Like

By the time the statewide rifle opener hits on October 24, this stops being a background consideration and becomes the default assumption. Multiple-day gaps in availability. Weekends that are off the table months in advance. Sellers who want their home shown by appointment only, with real notice, because they're not going to drop everything for a same-day request during the two weeks that matter most to them all year.

None of that has to slow a transaction down. It just means the calendar gets built with those weeks already blocked out, instead of getting rebuilt around them after a missed deadline. A seller who tells me in September which weeks in October are off-limits gets a listing strategy and a showing plan that respects that from day one. A buyer who flags the same thing gets an offer timeline that doesn't assume they're glued to their phone during opening weekend.

The Practical Version

If you're planning to list, buy, or are already under contract heading into archery or rifle season: say so, early, and say so specifically. Give dates, not "sometime in October." If you're working with an agent who hasn't asked, ask them how they plan around it — the answer tells you a lot about whether your calendar is going to hold up once the valley empties out for a few weeks.

This isn't about slowing anything down. It's about building the plan around the parts of your life that don't move for a closing date, instead of finding out the hard way that they don't.

Do you have dates this fall where you know you'll be out of range — and does your current plan already account for them, or is it going to find out the hard way?

item.title: The Sibling Buyout: How Heirs Actually Price One Person Keeping the House
item.dc:creator: Ryan Berner
item.description: When one sibling wants to keep an inherited Flathead Valley home and the others want their share, the disagreement almost always starts with the number. Here's how that number actually gets set — and where buyouts go wrong.
item.content:encoded:
The Sibling Buyout: How Heirs Actually Price One Person Keeping the House

Three siblings inherit their parents' house in the Flathead Valley. Two are ready to sell. One wants to stay — maybe they've been the one checking on the place, maybe it's just home. Everyone agrees, in principle, that a buyout is the fair answer.

Then someone asks the question that actually matters: bought out at what price? And that's where the agreement usually stops.

If you're the personal representative or one of the heirs trying to work this out, here's how that number gets set in practice, and the places this quietly falls apart.

First, the disclaimer that has to come first: I'm a real estate agent, not an attorney or a CPA. Montana probate has its own rules about distribution, timing, and what a personal representative needs court approval to do, and those rules depend on the will and the specifics of the estate. What follows is meant to sharpen the questions you bring to your attorney and CPA, not to replace their answers.

Whose number counts, and whose doesn't

Every sibling buyout I've seen struggle started with the same mistake: someone's opinion of value got treated as the value.

The sibling who wants to keep the house has every incentive to think it's worth less. The siblings being bought out have every incentive to think it's worth more. The county assessor's number reflects tax policy, not market value, and is often years behind. A sibling's memory of "what the Petersons got for their place down the road" isn't a comparable, it's a rumor.

None of those numbers can settle a disagreement, because none of them are neutral. The fix is the same one that works in every estate sale: an independent, licensed appraisal — often the same date-of-death appraisal the estate needs for tax purposes anyway. It isn't a perfect substitute for what the house would fetch on the open market, but it's defensible, it's in writing, and it's nobody's opinion. Get it before anyone states a number out loud. Positions harden fast once a figure is on the table, even an informal one.

How the buying sibling actually pays for it

Once there's a value, the next fight is usually about how the buyout gets financed — and this is where I see families lose months.

The sibling keeping the house typically needs to refinance the inherited property into a new mortgage in their own name, using the loan proceeds to pay the other heirs their share. That means qualifying on their own income and their own debts, with a fresh appraisal from a lender who has zero interest in the estate's peace and quiet. A number the family agreed on informally can come in lower — or higher — once a bank's appraiser looks at the same house. Confirm financing capacity in week one, not after everyone has emotionally settled on a figure. I've watched a sibling agree to "buy the others out," spend two months telling the family it was handled, and then fail to qualify for the loan — which restarts the entire negotiation from a much angrier starting point.

The costs that don't exist in a normal sale

A sibling buyout isn't a normal purchase, and pricing it like one skips real costs that need to be assigned somewhere.

There's no listing agent commission, but there's often a new appraisal fee, refinance closing costs, title work, and sometimes a small transfer or recording cost depending on how the deed moves. Someone has to decide whether those come off the top of the buyout price, get split evenly among all heirs, or land entirely on the sibling keeping the house. There's no universal answer — it's a negotiation — but it needs to be decided explicitly and in writing, not assumed. The estates that avoid resentment later are the ones where this got settled before the closing, not argued about after.

When the appraisal comes in lower than someone expected

This happens more than families expect, and it's worth planning for before it does. If the independent appraisal lands below what a sibling was counting on, the instinct is to argue the number. Resist that. The more useful conversation is what the family does with the number: does the buyout proceed at the appraised value, does the family get a second opinion, does the sibling staying in the house need to bring cash to the table to make the others whole. Decide the process for handling a disappointing number before you have one — it's a much calmer conversation in the abstract than it is once a specific figure is sitting in front of everyone.

Probate puts a clock on all of this

Montana probate timelines add real pressure here that a normal home sale doesn't have. Depending on the type of probate and the estate's obligations, there can be deadlines for distributing assets or closing out the estate that don't wait for siblings to reach comfortable consensus on financing. That's exactly why I push families to get the appraisal and the financing conversation moving in parallel, early, rather than sequentially — waiting for one before starting the other is often what turns a manageable few months into a year.

So here's the question worth asking before the next family conversation: has anyone actually gotten an independent number yet, or is everyone still negotiating from a guess?

I don't take sides between heirs. item.title: Insurance First, Offer Second: What Flathead Buyers Skip Until It's Too Late
item.dc:creator: Ryan Berner
item.description: Most Flathead Valley buyers call an insurance carrier the week before closing. Here's why calling before you write an offer protects your deal instead.
item.content:encoded:
Insurance First, Offer Second: What Flathead Buyers Skip Until It's Too Late

If you're house-hunting in Kalispell or Whitefish right now, you've probably spent real hours comparing floor plans, mudroom storage, and which elementary school a property feeds into. Here's a question that matters just as much and gets asked far too late: have you called an insurance carrier about this specific property yet?

Most buyers haven't. Most buyers call for the first time the week before closing — sometimes after the offer is already signed, sometimes after the lender has already asked for proof of coverage and started the clock ticking. By then, a bad quote isn't a data point. It's a problem sitting on top of your closing date.

Why This Gets Skipped

It's not that buyers don't care about insurance. It's that insurance doesn't feel urgent during the search phase. You're focused on whether the house works for your life — the number of bedrooms, the commute, whether the shop has 220V. Insurance feels like paperwork you'll deal with later, the same category as picking a title company or scheduling movers.

The problem is that in the Flathead Valley, insurance isn't always paperwork. On certain properties, it's a gatekeeper.

What Actually Moves a Quote Here

A lot of Flathead Valley inventory sits in or near the wildland-urban interface — timbered lots, homes backed up to national forest, properties out toward Foys Lake, Herron Park, or the benches above Whitefish where the tree line comes right up to the house. Carriers underwrite those properties differently than they underwrite a flat lot in town, and a few specific things drive the number:

Roof age and material. A 20-year-old roof, or a wood-shake roof anywhere near timber, is one of the fastest ways to get a declined quote rather than just an expensive one. Some carriers won't write wildfire-zone coverage on wood shake at any price. If a listing photo shows shake shingles and you're picturing it as a future re-roof project, that project may need to happen before closing, not after.

Defensible space. Carriers increasingly ask about the buffer between the structure and the nearest trees or brush — sometimes with a formula, sometimes with an inspector or a satellite-imagery review. A beautifully wooded lot that reads as private and quiet to you can read as high-risk to an underwriter if the canopy comes within a few feet of the eaves.

Water source, for rural properties. Homes on well and septic, especially without a fire hydrant within a set distance, get asked about static water sources — a pond, a cistern, proximity to a creek. It's not a question most buyers expect, and it's not one most listing agents volunteer.

Prior claims history on the property, not just on you. A house with a claims history the seller didn't necessarily disclose can affect your quote regardless of your own record.

Any one of these can turn a routine quote into a declined one, a high-deductible one, or a "we can write it, but not at the number you budgeted" one.

Why This Belongs on the Pre-Offer List

Here's the sequence that causes trouble: buyer falls for a property, writes an offer, offer gets accepted, buyer finally calls for insurance during the option period or right before closing, and the quote comes back either unaffordable or the carrier declines to write it altogether. Now the buyer is scrambling for a second or third carrier with a closing date already on the calendar and a lender who needs proof of coverage to fund. That pressure rarely produces a better outcome — it produces whatever policy is available in time, at whatever price.

Compare that to calling a carrier — or better, two or three — before you write the offer. You're not committing to anything. You're gathering the one piece of information that can quietly kill a deal a home inspection would never catch, because a home inspector checks whether the roof leaks, not whether an insurance company will cover it. Ten minutes on the phone with a local agent who knows Flathead County underwriting, using the listing's address and rough details, tells you what you're walking into before you're financially attached to the outcome.

This isn't about being pessimistic on a home you're excited about. It's about protecting the offer you're about to make — treating insurance as due diligence with the same seriousness you'd give well flow or septic inspection, not as a closing-week formality.

The Practical Version

Before you write on a property in a wooded or rural setting: get a preliminary quote or at least a same-day phone read from a local carrier. Ask directly about roof material and age, defensible space requirements, and water source if it's on well. If a property is going to be hard to insure, you want that answer during your due-diligence window — when it still has leverage in the negotiation, or a walk-away option attached to it — not after you've waived contingencies.

This article covers general practice and is not insurance or legal advice — coverage availability and underwriting requirements vary by carrier and change over time; confirm specifics with a licensed insurance agent before writing an offer.

item.title: The Buyout Loan: Why Refinancing to Keep the House Is Harder Than It Sounds
item.dc:creator: Ryan Berner
item.description: "I'll just refinance and keep the house" is the plan almost every spouse floats first in a Montana divorce — and the one that falls apart the most. Here's the sequence a buyout refinance actually requires, step by step.
item.content:encoded:
The Buyout Loan: Why Refinancing to Keep the House Is Harder Than It Sounds

If you've said the words "I'll just refinance and keep the house" out loud to your attorney, you're not alone. It's the first plan almost every spouse floats in a Flathead Valley divorce. It's also, more often than any other plan, the one that quietly falls apart three months later — not because anyone changed their mind, but because nobody walked through what a buyout refinance actually requires before it got written into the settlement.

This isn't legal or tax advice, and it isn't a case for keeping the house or selling it. Your attorney and your lender own those numbers. What follows is the sequence — the steps a buyout refinance has to clear, in order, and where each one tends to snag.

You're qualifying alone now, on one income

The mortgage on the house was likely approved on two incomes and two sets of debts. A buyout refinance has to qualify on one of each. That sounds obvious stated plainly, but it's the step most people haven't priced out before it's in the settlement agreement — a debt-to-income ratio that worked fine for a household of two can miss the mark for a household of one, especially once spousal support, if any, is added to the liability side of that math rather than the income side, or not counted as income at all depending on how long it's guaranteed to continue. The lender runs this number. It doesn't care what the decree says should happen — only whether the person keeping the house can actually carry the loan alone.

The appraisal doesn't know what number is in the settlement

Somewhere in the settlement conversation, a home value got agreed to — sometimes from a comparative market analysis, sometimes from a number one spouse remembered from three years ago, sometimes from what felt fair. The refinance doesn't use that number. It uses a fresh appraisal, ordered fresh, valuing the house as of today.

If that appraisal comes in lower than the figure written into the settlement, the equity the other spouse is owed doesn't shrink to match — but the amount available to refinance against does. That gap has to be closed with cash, a renegotiated split, or a different plan entirely, and it's a far better conversation to have before the settlement is signed than after the appraisal report lands.

The spouse being bought out is still on the loan — and the liability — until closing actually happens

This is the one that catches people off guard. A settlement agreement can say the house belongs to one spouse and the other is being bought out. That agreement does not remove either name from the existing mortgage. Only the new loan closing does that. Until the refinance actually funds, both spouses remain contractually liable for the original mortgage, whatever the decree says about who's responsible for what. A late payment during that window shows up on both credit reports. "The divorce is final" and "the refinance closed" are two different dates, and the gap between them is where risk sits for the spouse who's supposed to be out.

Timing the closing against a deadline that doesn't move for a lender

Settlement agreements often include a date: refinance and remove the other spouse's name by such-and-such, or the house gets listed instead. Lenders don't work around court deadlines — they work through underwriting timelines, appraisal scheduling, and title work, the same as any other refinance. Building a 30-day cushion between the loan's realistic closing date and the settlement's deadline isn't overcautious. It's the difference between a clean transition and a scramble that lands back in front of the judge.

When the refinancing spouse can't qualify for the full amount

Sometimes the numbers simply don't work — income doesn't support the loan amount needed to pay out the other spouse's share, even with the house's full equity behind it. This isn't a failure, and it isn't a dead end. It's information, and it usually means one of a few paths: a smaller buyout paired with a payment plan for the remainder, a co-signer, a longer runway before refinancing is attempted again, or — for some couples — selling the house and splitting the proceeds turns out to be the cleaner outcome for both people once the refinance math is actually run rather than assumed.

A question worth asking before it's in writing

If your settlement includes a buyout refinance, has anyone actually run the numbers — income, appraisal, timeline — or is the plan resting on what felt fair in a conversation?

That's not a question your attorney can answer alone, and it's not one I can answer instead of a lender. But it's the question worth asking before the number goes into the agreement, not after.

item.title: 62 to 77: What the Extra Two Weeks on Market Costs Flathead Sellers
item.dc:creator: Ryan Berner
item.description: Kalispell's median days on market has stretched from 62 a year ago to 77 today. Here's what that extra two weeks actually costs a seller, and what to do about it this week instead of waiting for spring.
item.content:encoded:
Sixty-two. Seventy-seven.

Those are Kalispell's median days on market a year ago and today, respectively (source: Movoto Kalispell, MT market data, period through August 2026, page updated September 21, 2026). Fifteen extra days doesn't sound dramatic until you sit with what actually happens inside those two weeks — and it's worth sitting with, because a lot of sellers on the sidelines right now are measuring the wrong number entirely.

The Numbers First

Kalispell, current snapshot: median sale price $699,000, 693 active listings, median days on market 77 — up from 62 a year ago (source: Movoto, data through August 2026, updated September 21, 2026).

On rate, the Freddie Mac Primary Mortgage Market Survey put the 30-year fixed at 6.95% for the week of September 17, 2026, up from 6.76% the week before (source: Freddie Mac PMMS).

That's the whole picture in two sentences. Everything below is what a seller actually does with it.

What "Two Extra Weeks" Really Means

A house that used to find a buyer in about nine weeks now takes closer to eleven. On paper that reads like a rounding error. In practice, those fifteen days are rarely quiet ones.

They're the window where a listing crosses from "new and interesting" to "still here" in a buyer's saved-search feed. They're the stretch where an agent previewing for a client starts asking why it hasn't sold yet, before ever asking what it's worth. And more often than not, they're the days where a price reduction gets discussed — not because the house changed, but because the calendar did.

Fifteen days by itself won't sink a listing. What sinks a listing is a seller who doesn't know those fifteen days are now the baseline, and who reads every one of them as evidence something is wrong with the house instead of evidence the whole market shifted underneath it.

The Mistake: Measuring Against Last Year

The seller who gets hurt in this market isn't the one who's slow to sell. It's the one comparing this listing to a house that sold in June of last year, in nine weeks, at full price — and quietly deciding their own house is underperforming when it's actually tracking right at this year's median.

That comparison is the trap. Sixty-two days was last year's market. Seventy-seven is this one. A house sitting at day 60 today isn't behind schedule. It's roughly on pace. The seller who doesn't know that will start second-guessing the price around week seven, right when patience was the correct answer.

The fix isn't complicated: know the current median before you list, not the one you remember from a friend's sale eighteen months ago.

What a Longer Market Actually Changes

A slower median doesn't just mean more waiting. It changes the mechanics of the deal itself, in three specific ways worth planning for before you're in the middle of them:

More price reductions happen before contract, not after listing. With more inventory for buyers to compare against, a house that opens a touch high has more competition sitting right next to it on the same search page. The reduction that used to be rare is now closer to routine — plan for the possibility rather than treating it as a failure if it happens.

Appraisal-gap language gets softer. When homes were moving in nine weeks, buyers waived contingencies to win multiple-offer situations. At 77 days, multiple offers are less common, and buyers have more room to ask for an appraisal contingency rather than bridging a gap in cash. Sellers should expect more negotiation on that clause, not less.

Buyers have more to compare you against. Six hundred ninety-three active listings means a buyer touring your house toured, or at least screened, several others this week. The house that shows clean, prices realistically against current comparables, and photographs well in the light it actually has is the one that doesn't need the full 77 days to find its buyer.

What This Means for You This Week

If you're already on the market and past day 60, don't panic — check your pace against 77, the current number, not 62. If you're inside that window, you're not behind. If you're well past it, that's the moment for an honest look at price against what's actually closed nearby in the last 30 days, not what's still asking.

If you're waiting for spring hoping the market "comes back" to last year's pace, ask yourself what specifically you think changes between now and April. Rates aren't the lever — they've moved up, not down, over the past two weeks, and a rate drop would bring more buyers into every listing at once, not just yours. The seller who prices correctly and lists into a quieter fall often does better than the one who waits for a crowded spring.

So here's the actual question worth asking this week: do you know what your house is worth against what's closed in the last 30 days — not what's currently asking, what closed — or are you still pricing off a market that expired sometime last year?

item.title: When the Right Advice Is \"Don't\"
item.dc:creator: Ryan Berner
item.description: Why a Flathead Valley agent whose income depends on a closing sometimes has to argue against one — and why the clients who hear it are the ones who send people.
item.content:encoded:
When the Right Advice Is "Don't"

When was the last time someone in a commission-based job told you not to do the thing that pays them?

It doesn't come up much, because it isn't supposed to. The incentive in this business runs one direction: a transaction closes, or it doesn't, and only one of those outcomes puts money in an agent's pocket. So the harder conversations this month — the ones about planning a sale around a divorce timeline, sequencing an estate through probate, reading an offer past the headline number — have all assumed the client and the agent want the same thing: to get to closing, cleanly. This one is about what happens when they don't.

The Job Nobody Puts on the Business Card

Most of real estate is exactly what it looks like — pricing, marketing, negotiating, managing a timeline. But underneath that is a smaller, less comfortable job: telling a client that the deal sitting in front of them, the one they've already started picturing themselves living in or hoping to fund with, isn't the one to do. Not because the paperwork is wrong. Because the fit is.

That instinct isn't new to real estate for me. Years spent making calls where the cost of being wrong was measured in more than money teaches you a specific discipline: separate what you want to be true from what the situation is actually telling you, say the uncomfortable thing early, and let the decision-maker decide with full information rather than a comfortable version of it. Applied here, that means an agent's job isn't just to get a client to the table. It's to tell them, plainly, when the table isn't worth sitting at.

Three Situations, Told Without Names

None of what follows is one specific client — these are composites, built from patterns that show up often enough to be worth writing down.

The house that checks every box except one. A buyer finds a place with the right bedroom count, the right school district, the right price, and a driveway that turns into a sheet of ice every winter because of how the lot sits relative to the sun. On a July showing, nobody notices. The box-checking is satisfying enough that the one real problem gets waved off as something to "figure out later." Later, for a lot of buyers, means a house they resent by February. Pointing that out before the offer goes in doesn't kill every deal like it — some buyers hear it and go forward anyway, eyes open, which is a fine outcome. But they heard it first.

The offer that should be countered, not accepted. A seller gets a number that's close enough to asking that the temptation is to just take it and be done — especially after a slower stretch on the market. Sometimes that instinct is right. Sometimes the offer is soft in a way the headline price hides: a long due-diligence period, financing that hasn't been verified past a form letter, a closing date that doesn't actually work for the seller's own next move. Accepting fast isn't the same as accepting well, and a seller who's tired of waiting is exactly the seller who needs someone to slow the moment down for thirty seconds before signing.

The purchase that pencils out and shouldn't be stretched for. A buyer can technically qualify for a number that leaves almost nothing left over once the mortgage, taxes, insurance, and the realities of an older home are all sitting on the same monthly statement. The math works on paper. It's the kind of math that works right up until a furnace fails in January or a job gets shakier than expected. Telling a buyer that qualifying for a number isn't the same as being able to live inside it comfortably is not the advice that gets an offer written today. It's usually the advice that keeps someone in their house five years from now.

What It Actually Costs to Say No

Arguing against a transaction is not free for the person doing it. It costs a commission that might not come back around, at least not from that specific deal. It sometimes costs a client relationship if the advice lands wrong or the client wasn't ready to hear it. And it never comes with a thank-you in the moment — nobody feels grateful for being told to wait, or to pass, or to counter instead of just taking the win.

What it buys instead is longer and quieter: a client who, three years later, is still glad they didn't buy that house, or that they held out for a real offer instead of the first one. Those are the clients who refer people. Not because the transaction was exciting, but because someone was willing to be the person in the room whose job wasn't just to get the deal done.

What This Actually Sounds Like

It's rarely dramatic. It sounds like "before you write this offer, let's talk about what the driveway does every winter." It sounds like "I'd counter this, and here's specifically why." It sounds like "you qualify for this, and I want to make sure you also want to live inside it." None of it is a war story. It's a standard, applied the same way whether the deal is easy or hard: say the true thing before the offer is signed, not after.

If you're in the middle of a decision right now and something about it doesn't sit right — even if you can't quite name what — that instinct is worth a conversation before it's worth an offer.
